claim: Our count from the Mains question bank: questions naming the monsoon (or El Nino with the monsoon) appear in 7 of the 11 sittings 2016-2026 (2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2022, 2023, 2026), 10 questions or parts in GS I and the Geography optional
source: Our own count, research/upsc/_pyq/mains/questions.csv (text search for 'monsoon' or 'El Nino'), from UPSC's question papers
note: A text search can miss a question that describes the monsoon without the word; the count is a floor.

claim: Geography optional Paper I (2018) prints 'Time Allowed: Three Hours, Maximum Marks: 250'; by our arithmetic a 20-mark question gets about 14 minutes (180 x 20 / 250 = 14.4)
source: UPSC, Civil Services (Main) Examination 2018, Geography Paper I, cover page
note: Our arithmetic; UPSC sets no time per question.

claim: UPSC prints no word limit for optional-paper questions such as 2018 Geography Paper I Q3(a); its GS papers print limits (150 and 250 words)
value: no word limit on optional questions
source: UPSC, Civil Services (Main) Examination 2018, Geography Paper I, instructions and page 3
note: Our working budget for a 20-mark optional answer is our choice.

claim: Article 368(4), inserted by s.55 of the 42nd Amendment (1976): no amendment 'shall be called in question in any court on any ground'; Article 368(5): 'no limitation whatever on the constituent power of Parliament' to amend. Both still printed, footnoted as declared invalid in Minerva Mills
source: Legislative Department, The Constitution of India (as on 10 Sep 2026), Article 368
note: Quoted words are the printed text.

claim: GS Paper II (2019) prints 'Time Allowed: Three Hours, Maximum Marks: 250' and that answers to questions 11 to 20 should be in 250 words; by our arithmetic a 15-mark question gets about 11 minutes (180 x 15 / 250 = 10.8)
source: UPSC, Civil Services (Main) Examination 2019, General Studies Paper II, cover and instructions
note: Our arithmetic; UPSC sets no time per question.

claim: Minerva Mills (1980), headnote [240C-E]: 'The power to destroy is not a power to amend'; since the Constitution conferred a limited amending power, Parliament cannot enlarge that very power into an absolute power; a limited amending power is one of the basic features
value: limited power is a basic feature
source: Supreme Court of India, Minerva Mills Ltd v Union of India, (1980) 3 SCC 625, judgment text (copy saved from Indian Kanoon because the Court's own search is behind a CAPTCHA, POL06-J02)
note: Read in the saved judgment text; the question's wording echoes this passage but is not a verbatim quote.
